summary: Rotate which slice is held back so every row is tested once.
headline: Many small exams instead of one
overview: Cut the data into k slices. Train on k − 1 of them, test on the one left out, and repeat until every slice has had a turn.
The average is a steadier estimate than any one split. The spread between folds tells you how much to trust it.

break.label: Break it
break.explains: Try 40 single splits and report only the best-looking. The number is real, and it is also a lie about how the model will do.

check.question: You run many experiments and report the best score you saw. What went wrong?
options: The score is optimistic because you picked the luckiest result

realLife: Teams that report the best of many runs ship models that quietly underperform their slide.
data: The same forty points as the last lesson, shuffled once with a fixed seed, with a degree-5 polynomial. Fold sizes follow scikit-learn's KFold rule: the first n mod k folds get one extra row.
maths: The model is refitted for each fold. The spread is the standard deviation of the k fold errors. Choosing the best of many splits adds selection bias on top of ordinary noise.
code:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold
scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0))
print(scores.mean(), scores.std())
